definition: Granular computing is an emerging computing paradigm of information processing that concerns the processing of complex information entities called "information granules", which arise in the process of data abstraction and derivation of knowledge from information or data.
details: Generally speaking, information granules are collections of entities that usually originate at the numeric level and are arranged together due to their similarity, functional or physical adjacency, indistinguishability, coherency, or the like. At present, granular computing is more a theoretical perspective than a coherent set of methods or principles. As a theoretical perspective, it encourages an approach to data that recognizes and exploits the knowledge present in data at various levels of resolution or scales. In this sense, it encompasses all methods which provide flexibility and adaptability in the resolution at which knowledge or information is extracted and represented.

explainer.lead: Granular computing is a way of thinking about information at different levels of detail. It groups related pieces of data into larger units, called information granules, so that useful knowledge can be found without always working at the finest level.

tiers.eli5: Imagine sorting a box of crayons by color instead of examining every crayon separately. You can talk about the red group or the blue group when a broad picture is enough, then look at individual crayons when you need more detail. Granular computing uses the same idea to turn data into useful knowledge.
tiers.practitioner: Treat granular computing as a design perspective: group entities by properties such as similarity, adjacency, or indistinguishability, then choose a resolution suited to the information being extracted. The central pitfall is expecting a single coherent method or fixed grouping procedure; the perspective instead accommodates different methods and levels of representation.
tiers.paperLevel: An information granule G is a collection of entities, often originating at the numeric level, grouped by relations such as similarity, functional or physical adjacency, indistinguishability, or coherency. Granular computing studies abstraction and knowledge derivation through representations at multiple resolutions or scales. It is currently a theoretical perspective rather than a coherent set of methods or principles.

explainer.example: Given the numeric measurements 1.0, 1.1, 1.2, 9.8, and 10.1, similar values can form two granules: {1.0, 1.1, 1.2} and {9.8, 10.1}. A coarse representation can describe them as a low group and a high group, while the original measurements remain available when finer detail is required.
explainer.intuition: Detail is not always helpful: sometimes a broad group reveals more than many individual values. Information granules let a representation move between broad and fine views according to the knowledge needed.
howItWorks: Begin with individual information entities, often numeric data.
Group related entities using similarity, adjacency, indistinguishability, coherency, or a related criterion.
Treat each resulting collection as an information granule.
Abstract or represent knowledge using those granules.
Change the resolution when a broader or finer view is needed.
explainer.whyItMatters: It emphasizes flexibility in the resolution at which information is represented and knowledge is extracted. That can help an approach exploit structure at different scales instead of forcing every task into one fixed level of detail.
misconceptions: It is not yet one coherent set of methods or principles.
An information granule is not necessarily a group of similar values; adjacency, indistinguishability, and coherency can also motivate grouping.
Using granules does not mean discarding every finer level of representation.
